      II.  Applicable Law                                                    

           A.  Motions in limine                                             

3        A motion in limine is “a procedural mechanism to limit in advance testimony or evidence in a 
4   partic ular area.” United States v. Heller, 551 F.3d  1108, 1111 (9th Cir. 2009). A party files a motion 
5   in lim ine to exclude anticipated prejudicial evidence before the evidence is introduced at trial. See 
6   Luce v . United States, 469 U.S. 38, 40 n.2 (1984). A court has the power to grant such motions 
7   pursua nt to its “inherent authority to manage trials,” even though such rulings are not explicitly 
8   author ized by the Federal Rules of Evidence. Id. at 41 n.4 (citation omitted). Regardless of a court’s 
9   initial  decision on a motion in limine, it may revisit the issue at trial. Id. at 41–42 (“[E]ven if nothing 
10   unexp ected happens at trial, the district judge is free, in the exercise of sound judicial discretion, to 
11   alter a  previous in limine ruling.”).                                   
12

13

14

15                                                                            
    (B). This written report must contain, in part: (1) a complete statement of all opinions expressed by 
16                                                                            
    the witness and the “basis and reasons for them”; (2) the facts and data used by the witness in 
17                                                                            
    forming his or her opinions; and (3) the exhibits that will be used to support or summarize the 
18                                                                            
    opinions. FED. R. CIV. P. 26(a)(2)(B)(i)–(iii).                          
19                                                                            
20          C.  Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16                            
21

22

22   (quoting FED. R. EVID. 702). While Courts may reject wholly speculative or unfounded testimony, it

           E.  Federal Rules of Evidence 401 and 402                         
4                                                                            
5        Federal Rule of Evidence 402 explicitly prohibits the inclusion of “irrelevant” evidence. FED. 
6   R. EV ID. 402. The Rule dictates that “[r]elevant evidence is admissible unless any of the following 
7   provid es other: the United States Constitution; a federal statute; these rules; or other rules prescribed 
8   by the  Supreme Court. Irrelevant evidence is not admissible.” FED. R. EVID. 402. 
9        Federal Rule of Evidence 401 prescribes what evidence qualifies as relevant. FED. R. EVID. 
10   401. I t provides that evidence is relevant if: “(a) it has any tendency to make a fact more or less 
11   proba ble than it would be without the evidence; and (b) the fact is of consequence in determining the 
12   action .” Id. 401(a)–(b); see also Crawford v. City of Bakersfield, 944 F.3d 1070, 1077 (9th Cir. 
13   2019)  (“Deciding whether a fact is of consequence in determining the action generally requires 
14   consid ering the substantive issues the case presents.” (internal quotation marks omitted)). Courts 
15   have r ecognized that Rule 401’s “basic standard of relevance . . . is a liberal one.” Crawford, 944 
16   F.3d a t 1077.

           F.  Federal Rule of Evidence 403                                  
18

19

20                                                                            
    prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay, wasting time, or needlessly 
21                                                                            
    presenting cumulative evidence.” District courts have broad discretion in assessing admissibility 
22                                                                            
    under Rule 403. Sprint/United Mgmt. Co. v. Mendelsohn, 552 US 379, 384 (2008) (finding “wide 
23                                                                            
    discretion” necessary because Rule 403 “requires an on-the-spot balancing of probative value and 
24                                                                            
    prejudice, potentially to exclude . . . evidence that already has been found to be factually relevant”) 
25                                                                            
    c ert. denied, 142 S. Ct. 2834 (2022) (“A district court’s Rule 403 determination is subject to great 

1   deference, because the considerations arising under Rule 403 are susceptible only to case-by-case 

    determinations, requiring examination of the surrounding facts, circumstances, and issues.”).   

           G. Federal Rules of Evidence 801, 802, and 805                    

3        As defined by Federal Rule of Evidence 801, “hearsay” is an out-of-court statement that: (1) 
4   the de clarant does not make while testifying at th e current trial or hearing; and (2) a party offers in 
5   eviden ce to prove the truth of the matter asserted in the statement.” FED. R. EVID. 801. A statement 
6   includ es “a person’s oral assertion, written assertion, or nonverbal conduct, if the person intended it 
7   as an  assertion.” Id. Under Federal Rule of Evidence 802, hearsay evidence is inadmissible unless 
8   otherw ise provided by a federal statute, the Federal Rules of Evidence, or other rules prescribed by 
9   the Su preme Court. FED. R. EVID. 802. Hearsay within hearsay is likewise inadmissible unless each 
10   part o f the combined statements conforms with an exception to the rule against hearsay. FED. R. 
11   EVID.  805.
